title: Security best practices: passwords, MFA & encryption
summary: Learn the everyday security controls a Tier 1 technician enforces: strong password and account policies, multi-factor authentication, and full-disk encryption with BitLocker.
objectives: Explain why length and uniqueness beat complexity in modern password policy
Configure local account and lockout policies from the command line
Describe how multi-factor authentication stops stolen-password attacks
Enable and check BitLocker full-disk encryption with manage-bde
Save and use a BitLocker recovery key during a lockout
Apply the principle of least privilege to user accounts

quiz.q: Which password policy gives the best real-world protection against guessing and reuse attacks?
options: Force a change every 30 days with three special characters
Require long, unique passphrases and screen against known-breached passwords
Require exactly eight characters with one capital letter
Disable lockout so users never get blocked
quiz.why: Modern guidance (NIST and Microsoft) favours length and uniqueness over forced rotation and arbitrary complexity, and blocking known-breached passwords stops reuse attacks.

quiz.q: A user's password was phished. What single control would most likely have stopped the attacker from logging in?
quiz.why: MFA requires a second factor the attacker does not have, so a stolen password alone is not enough to sign in.

options: Data being read from a lost or stolen drive
quiz.why: BitLocker provides full-disk encryption, so data on a lost or stolen drive cannot be read without the key or recovery key.

quiz.q: Which command shows the encryption status of all drives on a Windows machine?
quiz.why: manage-bde -status reports protection status, encryption percentage and method for each volume; the other commands lock, refresh policy, or list users.

quiz.q: In one sentence, define the principle of least privilege and give one example.
quiz.answer: Least privilege means giving each user only the access they need to do their job and nothing more — for example, making a normal user a standard account instead of a local administrator.
quiz.why: Limiting privileges shrinks the damage an attacker or mistake can cause, which is why standard accounts are the default and admin rights are granted only when needed.

quiz.q: Why should you save the BitLocker recovery key somewhere other than the encrypted machine itself?
quiz.answer: If you are locked out (for example after a TPM or firmware change) you need the recovery key to unlock the drive, and it is useless if it is stored only on the drive you cannot access.
quiz.why: The recovery key is the fallback when normal unlock fails, so it must live somewhere independent — a Microsoft account, Azure AD, a printout, or a USB key kept elsewhere.

resources.label: Microsoft Support — How to use multi-factor authentication

body_markdown:
## Why security is a Tier 1 job

Most breaches do not start with a clever hacker; they start with a weak password, a reused password, or a laptop left on a train. As a helpdesk technician you are the person who actually turns the controls on. Three controls cover the majority of real risk: strong **authentication**, **multi-factor authentication (MFA)**, and **encryption**. Learn these and you protect both the user and the business.

## Passwords and account policy

Forget the old advice about swapping letters for symbols every month. Modern guidance favours **length and uniqueness**: a long **passphrase** is both stronger and easier to remember than `P@ss1!`. You also want an **account lockout** so attackers cannot guess endlessly, and you want to follow **least privilege** — give users a standard account, not local administrator, unless they genuinely need it.

You can inspect and set local policy from the command line:

```cmd
net accounts
:: Lockout threshold: Never  -> set it
net accounts /lockoutthreshold:5 /lockoutduration:15

:: List local users and check who is an admin
net user
net localgroup administrators
```

Sample output:

```cmd
Lockout threshold:                 5
Lockout duration (minutes):        15
```

## Multi-factor authentication

A password is **something you know**. MFA adds **something you have** (a phone or token) or **something you are** (a fingerprint). Even if a password is phished, the attacker cannot complete the login without the second factor. As a technician you will help users enrol in an authenticator app, generate **backup codes**, and recover when a device is lost. The key teaching point for users: approve a prompt **only** when you are the one signing in.

## Full-disk encryption with BitLocker

**BitLocker** encrypts the whole drive so a lost or stolen laptop is just an expensive paperweight, not a data leak. On business machines it usually relies on the **TPM** chip to release the key automatically at boot. Check and enable it with `manage-bde`:

```powershell
# Check status of every drive
manage-bde -status

# Turn BitLocker on for C: and save the recovery key to a file
manage-bde -on C: -recoverypassword
```

Sample output:

```powershell
Volume C: [OSDisk]
    Conversion Status:    Used Space Only Encrypted
    Percentage Encrypted: 100.0%
    Protection Status:    Protection On
```

## Recovery keys — do not skip this

If the TPM, firmware, or boot configuration changes, BitLocker demands the **recovery key**. Save it somewhere off the machine: a Microsoft account, Azure AD/Entra, a printout, or a USB stick stored elsewhere. A recovery key locked inside the drive you cannot open is worthless.

```powershell
# Show the numeric recovery password / key protectors
manage-bde -protectors -get C:
```

## Your task

On a test or virtual machine: run `net accounts` and set a lockout threshold of 5 attempts; confirm the change. Then run `manage-bde -status` to record the encryption state of C:. If BitLocker is available, capture the recovery key with `manage-bde -protectors -get C:` and write where you would store it safely. Summarise in three bullet points how passwords, MFA and encryption each protect a different stage of an attack.

slides.narration: Welcome to lesson six. Security is not someone else's job on a helpdesk; it's yours. In this lesson we'll cover the three controls that stop most real-world attacks: strong passwords and account policy, multi-factor authentication, and full-disk encryption with BitLocker. By the end you'll be able to set a lockout policy, explain why M F A matters, and check encryption from the command line.

slides.title: The three controls that matter
bullets: Most breaches start with weak or reused passwords.
Or a lost laptop with unencrypted data.
Authentication, M F A, and encryption cover the bulk of risk.
You are the person who turns these on.

Three controls cover the majority of real risk: strong authentication, multi-factor authentication, and encryption. As a technician, you're the one who actually switches these on, so they matter.

slides.title: Passwords: length beats tricks
bullets: Long passphrases beat short complex passwords.
Block reused and known-breached passwords.
Add account lockout to stop guessing.
Apply least privilege: standard, not admin.
slides.narration: Forget the old advice about swapping letters for symbols every month. Modern guidance favours length and uniqueness. A long passphrase is both stronger and easier to remember. Add an account lockout so attackers can't guess forever, and follow least privilege: give users a standard account, not local administrator, unless they truly need it.

slides.title: Set account policy from the command line
bullets: net accounts shows current policy.
Set lockout threshold and duration.
net user lists local accounts.
Check who's in the administrators group.
slides.code:
net accounts /lockoutthreshold:5 /lockoutduration:15
net user
net localgroup administrators
slides.narration: You can inspect and set local policy from the command line. Type net accounts to see the current settings. To add a lockout, run net accounts slash lockout-threshold colon five, and lockout-duration colon fifteen. Then net user lists local accounts, and net localgroup administrators shows who actually has admin rights. Check that list; you'll often find more admins than you expect.

slides.title: Multi-factor authentication
bullets: Password = something you know.
MFA adds something you have or are.
A phished password alone can't log in.
Help users enrol and save backup codes.
slides.narration: A password is something you know. Multi-factor authentication adds something you have, like a phone, or something you are, like a fingerprint. So even if a password is phished, the attacker can't finish the login without that second factor. You'll help users enrol in an authenticator app and save backup codes. Teach them one rule: approve a prompt only when you are the one signing in.

slides.title: BitLocker: encrypt the whole drive
bullets: Encrypts the entire disk, not single files.
A stolen laptop becomes unreadable.
Often uses the TPM chip to unlock at boot.
Check status with manage dash b d e.
slides.narration: BitLocker encrypts the whole drive, so a lost or stolen laptop is just an expensive paperweight, not a data leak. On business machines it usually uses the T P M chip to release the key automatically at boot. To check it, run manage dash b d e, space dash status. That reports the protection status and how much of the drive is encrypted.

slides.title: Turning BitLocker on
bullets: Use manage dash b d e dash on for the drive.
Generate a recovery password.
Protection status should read 'Protection On'.
Encryption can run in the background.
slides.narration: To turn BitLocker on for the C drive, run manage dash b d e, space dash on, space C colon, space dash recovery-password. That encrypts the drive and creates a recovery password. When it finishes, the protection status reads Protection On. Encryption can keep running in the background while the user works, so you don't have to wait.

slides.title: Recovery keys — never skip
bullets: TPM or firmware changes trigger a recovery prompt.
Store the key OFF the machine.
Options: Microsoft account, Entra, print, USB.
A key locked on the drive is useless.
slides.narration: Here's the part people skip and regret. If the T P M, firmware, or boot configuration changes, BitLocker demands the recovery key. You must store that key off the machine: a Microsoft account, Azure Entra, a printout, or a U S B stick kept elsewhere. Run manage dash b d e, space dash protectors, space dash get, space C colon to see it. A recovery key locked inside the drive you can't open is worthless.

slides.title: Least privilege in practice
bullets: Default users to standard accounts.
Grant admin only when justified.
Smaller privileges mean smaller blast radius.
Review the admins group regularly.
slides.narration: One more habit: least privilege. Give each user only the access they need and nothing more. Default people to standard accounts, and grant administrator rights only when there's a real reason. Smaller privileges mean a smaller blast radius if an account is compromised or someone makes a mistake. Review the administrators group regularly and trim it.

slides.title: Recap & your task
bullets: Passwords: long, unique, with lockout.
MFA stops stolen-password logins.
BitLocker protects lost or stolen drives.
Always store the recovery key off-machine.
Task: set lockout, check manage dash b d e status.
slides.narration: Let's recap. Passwords should be long, unique, and protected with a lockout. M F A stops a stolen password from being enough to log in. BitLocker protects a lost or stolen drive, and you must always store the recovery key off the machine. Your task: on a test or virtual machine, run net accounts and set a lockout threshold of five, confirm it, then run manage dash b d e status to record the encryption state of C. If BitLocker is on, capture the recovery key and note where you'd store it safely. See you in lesson seven.
